utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 11th of November. I'd like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, the accused, Defence counsel, General Beneta, representatives of the OTP, as well as all the people assisting us. I believe Ms. Pinter would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Yesterday during the cross-examination by General Praljak a map was presented, an original map that we were unable to have photocopied yesterday. In the meantime we did so. It's on the board. I let the Prosecutor compare the original with the copy, and I would now like to ask for an IC number for the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Mr. Laws?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President, indeed, Your Honours, and everyone else in and around the courtroom. No objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The map shall be given Exhibit IC1101. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, let me give you the floor for the rest of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And good morning to you, General. Can we pick up where we left off yesterday, please, on the topic of the southern front and volunteers, and would you turn in the Prosecution's binder to Exhibit P04295, please. This is an order in respect of sending volunteers to the southern front, and it's from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and we can see that it's signed by the defence minister, Mr. Susak, and approved by General Bobetko. You can see that on the last page. We're going to look at a bit of its contents in a moment. It's an order about sending troops and MTS to the southern front. Can we just look first of all at the final paragraph, paragraph 7, which tell us amongst other things that involved in the coordination of this order is Brigadier Tole the chief of the HVO staff, as he was in -- as he's referred to there. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So we can deduce from that that it's something in relation to the HVO. And we'll look back now together at the body of the order. In paragraph 1 we learn that it's to create a reinforced battalion out of the volunteers from the 5th Guards Motorised Brigade, 1st Battalion, going to be sent to the southern front. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 it says that the battalion of volunteers shall be reinforced, and then it gives us the weaponry with which it's to be reinforced: 120-millimetre mortar battery, a six-weapon system with an anti-aircraft defence battery, a 76-millimetre gun battery which is a six-weapon system, 128-millimetre RAK platoon. What's an RAK platoon?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: RAK means two weapons, two artillery weapons, multiple-rocket launchers, 128-millimetre calibre. Every launcher with 12 barrels, with a crew of four men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we're getting three of those sent on this deployment. Two tank platoons from the 5th Guards Motorised Brigade armoured battalion with the entire crew, and at least three combat sets of ammunition, and then it goes on to talk about the combat sets being provided with the necessary MTS to go with them? So it's not just that the volunteers are going to be allowed to be deployed to the southern front, but they're going to be, on the face of it, taking with them this weaponry; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this order, they should be carrying this weaponry with them, but I want to emphasise it says here up to two tank platoons, which is not really properly termed, but it all depends on the order. From 0 to 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, you might have some comments to make about the language, but the sense of paragraph 2, I'm going to suggest to you, is that some heavily armed soldiers are being deployed. Is that right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that this reads that in addition to the troops the volunteers referred to in paragraph 1, weaponry is sent. I can't say heavy weaponry. This is infantry weapons save for this phrase, "up to two tank platoons," which is not infantry weapons. Obviously the author of this order was unsure how many weapons will be able to be sent. The rest of the weaponry can be handled by infantrymen, because this is included in infantry skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And the volunteers who have, on your evidence, asked to go to fight in Bosnia and Herzegovina, they happened to be volunteers who will be proficient in all of the skills necessary to operate this equipment that they're taking with them, the multiple-rocket launchers, the mortars, the anti-aircraft defence batteries, et cetera. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In a group of 200, 300 soldiers at that time, you would find men who are infantrymen whose specialisations covered all these skills apart from the tanks. That is not an infantry skill.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No. But the tanks and the other weaponry are going with the volunteers. Does that in any way change your evidence about the nature of this engagement of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any reason to question any of my previous evidence. In paragraph 1, as in the paragraph about reinforcements, I don't see any reason to change my previous evidence. Apart from this reference to tanks, it says "up to two platoons," because the author obviously wasn't unsure to what extent this order will be able to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's one thing for a soldier to say, I want to go and fight in Bosnia. I'm suggesting to you that it's quite another for the Croatian Army to say, yes, that's all right, and please take with you multiple-rocket launchers, mortars, tanks. That's not -- that's not something that happens with a volunteer, is it? That's a deployment. That's what I'm suggesting to you, General.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can also confirm to you that we did not send volunteers blindly, haphazardly in a danger. We equipped them properly so that they have a chance of functioning there rather than sending them empty-handed, without equipment, without weapons, without communications, somewhere where they would be stranded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Would you please look now at paragraph 4 of this document. It's over the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Laws. Just a question of information, Mr. Beneta. A tank platoon signifies how many vehicles, how many armoured vehicles per platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a tank - T-55 is mentioned here if I'm not mistaken - it will have a crew of four men. Yes, I know they had T-55 tanks. Perhaps at that time even M-84 with a crew of three. So a crew would be three to four men per artillery weapon, and that would make 9 to 12 men in a tank platoon, plus commanders, of course. That means 10 to 13. Or let me correct myself, 12, because the commander of a platoon is also a member of the crew. So it would be 9 to 12 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I had actually not asked the number of men but the number of tanks, of armoured vehicles. I take it that it is three, three tanks to one platoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, three tanks per platoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So six -- six tanks are dispatched.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour, how many tanks were sent. I don't know anything about this order. I'm just reading what it says, and it says, "up to two tank platoons." I read this as, "send from 0 to 2 tank platoons."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There is perhaps again a lack of precision in the translation, because the "up to" I do not find in the English text. Would you be so kind as to read the number 2 of the order, beginning with "banju dragovoljaca."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you've noticed that very well. It just says two in English. I'm reading the original though. It reads: "The battalion of volunteers shall be reinforced with a 120-millimetre mortar battery (six weapons), with an anti-aircraft defence battery of 20 or 14.5 millimetres, one 76-millimetre ZIS gun battery (six weapon systems), one multiple-rocket launcher platoon of 128-millimetres RAK (three weapons), up to two tank platoons from the armoured battalion of the 5th Guards --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, we have gotten to the right passage, and I can absolutely follow that the translation is wrong and you were right. So it would be up to -- mathematically up to six tanks, and you were quite correct in your answer. Thank you. Please, Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Over the page, please, General. Paragraph 4 and paragraph 5. "The 5th Guard Motorised Brigade commander and the assistant commander for political affairs shall be held responsible for the political preparations, conversations with all the volunteers, necessary explanations and motivation." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that that -- we saw a similar passage yesterday. That is describing preparing people who are being deployed. It's talking to them about motivation. It's talking to them about political preparation and explaining matters to them. It's deploying troops who need to be told why they're going there and what they can say whilst they're there. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not quite agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You nearly agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some aspects I agree, in others I don't, but I cannot give you a ratio or a percentage or even indicate that I agree more than not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. We'll take that answer. Thank you. The following paragraph just before we leave this document says that on its arrival in the port of Ploce, the volunteers battalion is to be put under the direct command of the HVO staff as the reserve. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Because that's the southern front, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ploce port, at any rate, is the southern front.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The HVO are operating in the southern front, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The southern front the Croatian Army is active, mainly in the Croatian part of the territory of the southern front, partly in the border belt on the side of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And here I see written, at least in what we've analysed so far of the text, that this group of volunteers, reinforced with some infantry weapons, maybe also tanks, maybe not, should be arriving in Ploce where they have to stay in reserve for intervening in an area of the southern front which is located, as I read here, possibly in the area of responsibility of the HVO, but they are still in the role of reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Would you turn to the next document, please, P06797.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Beneta, I'd like to get back to paragraph 5 of this document. I was waiting for the Prosecutor to finish before reviewing this paragraph with you again. Paragraph 5 states that these volunteers are all put under the commander of the HVO. This is crystal clear. On reading this document, I realise that fairly substantial reinforcements are provided since the tanks which were in Slavonia are going to cross the country in order to reach the southern front since they will be transported on a car ferry. So it's a large-scale operation which is being conducted here. Nobody can challenge the fact that this is an important operation. Now, in military terms, all these people are placed under the command of the HVO. Yesterday when I put a question to you relating to Kuwait and the Americans, you told me that normally speaking, in your view the American forces were to be subordinated to the Kuwaiti forces. I was going to follow up your answer with a question which I'm putting to you now. Now, considering what is happening in Afghanistan at the moment. NATO is in Afghanistan. I'm sure you're familiar with the situation. The US forces that are part of NATO are not under the command of Mr. Karzai. Let's take the case of Iraq for instance. Also, are the US forces under the command of the current Iraqi troops? You may respond by saying no. So military situations can be very different from one place to another. With these examples, I would like to know this: In this particular case we are talking about the southern front, and you have mentioned the theory of the single battle-field. How is it that all these units are being subordinated to the HVO? Why would the Croatian Army not still be in command? Why are these units placed under the command of the HVO. I find it difficult to understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I also said yesterday that it's thankless and easy to be misinterpreted to compare troops of a scale of the US forces that are deployed 10 to 12.000 miles away from the US territory with the forces of the Croatian Army which never, then or now, had anything similar in terms of forces, equipment, or power to justify such a comparison. Here again we see, indeed, that these forces of the Croatian Army, established as a volunteer unit, are placed at the disposal of the commander of the HVO. If you're asking me about the reasons why, the reasons lie in the official position of the political leadership of the Republic of Croatia and the pressure exerted by the international community for Croatia to refrain from interfering in the Bosnian war. If we had the same situation today and if I were in a decision-making position, I would go and protect the interests of Croatia wherever they are jeopardised, hitting directly at the centre of the threat. However, today in our current situation, our system is conceived in such a way that enables us to make alliances with plentiful grounds in the constitution, whereas at that time there were no such prerequisites. If you're asking me whether these people down there needed assistance and help, as a human being and as a military man I would always say yes, and I say yes, and I can only echo the words of General Praljak. We protected them the best way we could with everything we could within the limitations we had. And I have to emphasise that the role of the commander was one of the key roles, and I see that I'm frequently asked yesterday and today to put myself in the shoes of Mr. Kapular. I will say a few words about it here, with your leave, although I've seen some of these documents during proofing and decided that I had nothing to say about them. I never thought that I would be asked to explain someone else's decisions and acts. However, if a unit commander has friends there, family there, or any other ties to that area and is in a position to encourage people to volunteer and go help defend Bosnia and Herzegovina from aggression, then his unit will probably produce more volunteers. However, if a commander thinks he has his hands full on Croatian territory without going anywhere else, this position of the commander will also influence people and less of them will volunteer. Yesterday, I watched on television some sort of commemoration in the United States attended also by the president. I heard what he said. And if we go back to that document which reports on the protests of parents and friends of the men in the 5th Brigade and the punishment of those 26 men and the reasoning stated there, the language is practically the same as that used by the president of the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you, but you're going a bit too far in this kind of explanation. It sounds like pleading for the Defence. I think Mr. Laws should continue questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. The question was pending. I'm so sorry. The question was spending from Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Beneta, you are telling us that these volunteers went to the southern front for reasons. They had their own reasons. Very well. But as I was listening to you, I was wondering the following: What about the -- a tank crew member who hails from Slavonia? What business does he have going to the southern front? I don't know exactly how these crews were made up, but I assume that most of the tank crew members hailing from Slavonia had a very distant connection to this southern front. They were just executing an order. They were asked to come and reinforce units who were already deployed on the southern front and they obeyed. So you're telling us that they volunteered to go. Maybe so. We need to take a look at the breakdown of the tank crew members to seeks exactly whether they had a connection with Bosnia-Herzegovina or not, but I don't have all this at hand. I'm going to hand the floor back to Mr. Laws, but in your answer I wanted you to -- to explain why the HVO was in command, and you told us that it was because they were volunteers and it was up to the HVO to command them. At least that's what you gave us as an explanation. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The next document, please, General, is P06797. It's a document that was added overnight, in fact. And if it assists, we have a spare copy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Ah, you have it. Thank you, General. This is a document from the Welfare Administration Department of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. It's dated the 22nd of November, 1993, and it is an order which is said to be "based on the fact that there have been frequent remarks and complaints lately, related to correct and concrete way... carrying out duty, I hereby issue the following order." And if you look with me at the first paragraph of the order, I think we'll find it says: "1. To be very careful during filling out of death forms so that in the case of a person killed in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, one is supposed to fill in the southern battle-field and not the exact place of death. The matter is that this has been still happening, especially in the recent time ... some people are mentioning the name of the place of death as, for example, Mostar, Bugojno, or other places." Do you see that paragraph, General?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's an order that when people die in Mostar or in Bugojno or in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that mustn't be put on the death certificate. Instead, "Southern front" must be put on the death certificate. That's the effect of it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's being concealed. The truth is being concealed by this order, and I'm suggesting to you this: It's being concealed because its politically sensitive that Croatian troops are dying in Mostar and Bugojno and other places. Do you agree that that's a sensible interpretation of this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document is an example of the absurd situation in which we were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, could I interrupt you, because you told us a bit about the absurdity. I'm asking you a simple question. Do you agree that it is a sensible interpretation of this document, that the truth is being concealed because it is politically sensitive? Do you agree that that's a sensible interpretation of this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completely disagree. And I can state my reasons if you're willing to listen to me now. I'm sorry that you interrupted me five minutes ago, because I wanted to establish the link between what was said yesterday and Mr. Kapular, but I wasn't allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, you were -- you were stopped by the Judges when you wanted to talk about Mr. Kapular. Mr. Kapular is not involved in this document. You've given evidence over the course of two days about the fact that people were volunteering, and so being sent to the southern front because they wanted to go there. This document may or may not help us, but I want to take it in stages, and I've asked you whether you agree that the truth is being concealed because it's politically sensitive. You say you strongly disagree with that. Don't tell us about Mr. Kapular. Tell us why you disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for enabling me to say so now, and I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to go back to the issue that I haven't had the chance to deal with, haven't had the chance to exhaust. This document, if we understand the situation completely, absolutely cannot be connected to a political hiding of the fact that Croatian soldiers are being sent to the front in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This document is a consequence of a simultaneous establishment of a state, the laws and regulations that we had at the time, and the situation -- or, rather, reality which was not in line with that. If at the time a written -- there was no written evidence that the -- a soldier died in the southern front and exclusively in the Republic of Croatia, in other words, if there was written mention that he was killed even as little as 500 metres across the border, the killed man's family had no legal grounds for claiming a pension. This was written exclusively for social reasons, to enable the families to get what -- to get their due, because to us soldiers, it was so absurd that if we say that somebody was killed in the outskirts of Metkovic, on the Bosnian side of the border, then the family of that killed soldier cannot get what they would otherwise have been entitled to. So -- and if that man was the only one generating income for their family, the family would be left without anything. So on a daily basis we complained that this must not be done. I, too, drafted documents that this must be taken care of in the legislative way, but the -- they said that they didn't have time to do that. And in order to get to grips with the situation, they replied, "Well, then don't state that the man was killed across the border. Just state that he was killed at the southern front." And from a military point of view, the southern front was on both sides of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Mostar and Bugojno are both considerably more than 500 metres across the border, are they not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that there were individuals who even went as far as Bugojno as volunteers and remained Croatian soldiers. They retained that status. But the Croatian state considered it necessary to provide for his family if he got killed in Bosnia. I, too, had one or two such cases, and I still paid out wages for that killed soldier until the authorities resolved the situation. And I called his father, who was in Bosnia, and it was very difficult to bring him to Croatia to pay out to him the four -- his son's four last wages, although the son had already been killed. This is an interpretation of documents from the positions of a well-established state that has been functioning for hundreds of years. I beg you, do try to put yourself in the situation in 19 -- back in 1991 when the state wasn't yet fully established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, this is 1993. During 1992 and 1993, whilst you were deployed in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were a HV soldier, and you were being paid by Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And although Croatia could arrange to pay you your regular salary and could arrange the deployment of soldiers and weaponry as we saw in the last document, you're saying that it simply couldn't arrange benefits for those who died unless it said "Southern front" and not "Mostar." Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Benefits could be paid out if the official document read "Southern front." So if a soldier got killed in Croatian territory, then benefits could be paid out. This administration mentioned here, that also takes care of burying people or bodies --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We don't have very much time. We're not dealing with burying people at this stage. You've given your answer. Let's turn on to 4D00701.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. The question raised by Mr. Laws was essential. In his question, he put to you that according to him, according to the Prosecution, for political reasons the fact that Croatian troops were in Bosnia-Herzegovina was concealed, notably when they were killed in Mostar or Bugojno. There's a logic behind this point of view. But you are answering by saying that this was not the case, that it was just an administrative problem, because the administration of the Ministry of Defence, having noted that death certificates mentioned Mostar or Bugojno did not want to trigger off the procedure that should occur when a soldier dies on the battle-field. According to you, the Croatian law says that you can only get compensation if you died either on Croatian soil or on a Croatian front but not abroad. And then right at the end of your answer you said that this document came from the Ministry of Defence, from the welfare department in charge of burials, and I do note that -- and I do note welfare administration on this document. The -- Mr. Laws did not show you -- did not show you all the reasons behind this order, because in any military document, there is always reasons. In this document we see that there were remarks and complaints that had been made and that this was the reason why this order was actually issued. Now, here's my question: You're under oath, and you are telling us that this document is just the -- is just an explanation for administrative questions linked to the payment of compensation to families, because this payment can only be done if the troop actually died on Croatian soil or on the front, on the battlefront, but nowhere else. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have said the very things that I wanted to say, and I apologise if I didn't phrase it as well, because I was a bit upset, but you have summed it up perfectly. I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is your position. This is what I'm saying. I'm not saying that the conclusions -- we'll draw the same conclusion, but I tried to sum up your position. And I summed up also the Prosecution's position. Of course, both are different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to add a little question. Mr. Beneta, are you able to tell us where we find the rule that no compensation can be paid out if a soldier of the HV has been killed somewhere else than on the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot give you the exact reference such as the article, but I know that in the constitution and other subordinate legislation mention is made of the Croatian Army waging a defence war, and the -- the purpose of the war explicitly or implicitly was the defence of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Croatia. It was always about the territory of Croatia. This may be a law that was taken over from ex-Yugoslavia, because in order to maintain law and order in Croatia by a parliamentary decision, a series of legal acts was taken over from former Yugoslavia. I know when this was happening to me with people whose status had been frozen and they had left for Bosnia and Herzegovina temporarily, if they got killed the state didn't pay out to them what it should have, but I continued to disburse their salaries, although the men had been killed. But to my mind this was a lesser evil than leave their families without an income.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would -- would be led to draw the conclusion from your answer that dispatching Croatian soldiers to Bosnia and Herzegovina would not be exactly in conformity with the constitution. Is that a correct -- a correct thinking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they were not sent there. They were just enabled to go there, both individually and as a unit. I said as much yesterday. But they were not made to go there. They were not forced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Well, I -- I do not -- I cannot stop here, because I really feel that the very question which was raised by Judge Trechsel a few minutes ago, that is that the sending and dispatching Croatian soldiers of the HV to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I quote here, "would not be exactly in conformity with the constitution." And really, I feel that it is a bit difficult to accept what you, General Beneta, said, that they, that is the volunteers, "... they were not sent there. They were just enabled to go there, both individually and as a unit." I really feel that after so many documents what we have seen, it is a bit far-fetched to say that they were just enabled to go there. And I stop here, but I would like to -- just to mention that I have a kind of problem with that approach. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for rising now, but given the words of Judge Prandler, I need to point out the following: If I have studied the adjudicated facts properly, it is not an adjudicated fact that the Republic of Croatia deployed soldiers to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Secondly, considering the documents shown in this courtroom, the OTP has not proven that Croatian Army units were sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina in an organised manner. That remains to be proved yet, and we will prove that these -- they were really volunteers. I believe that this is a matter that deserves to be explained, but if what we heard a minute ago is the position of the Trial Chamber, then we need not introduce any more witnesses, but if we still have a chance as a Defence to prove our case, then I believe that the position of Judge Prandler should be explained, or otherwise should we take it that this matter has already been adjudicated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, no decision has been made, and you know this very well. Just -- you can see this with the numerous questions put by the Judges. And secondly, Judge Prandler very justly put a question to the witness, so let him answer. You're taking the floor, but what's important for us is the answer of the witness. Judge Prandler gave us his position. This is what this adversarial debate is all about, but you keep cutting the witness off. He was about to answer. Now, he might agree with Judge Prandler, or he might disagree, and he'll tell us why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, don't shout here when the President of the Court is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you can sentence me, but I'm not going to sit here like a log. You have anticipated the decision of this Trial Chamber. You said you don't believe. Well, it's your right not to believe, but I will not keep quiet about this because there is no evidence that units of the Croatian Army was -- were ever sent there. You can throw me out, you can punish me and throw me into gaol again. This will either be a trial or I will protest. I respect the Trial Chamber, but the Trial Chamber must also respect the people sitting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I do not want to, actually, to throw you out, and I have never suggested this kind of approach, number one. Number two, I have never spoken about adjudicated facts, and do I not know why Ms. Alaburic has take -- has mentioned this, and I only said that it is a bit difficult to believe that all those people were only allowed to go there, I mean to Herzegovina. It is what I said. It was not prejudged. Again, I didn't mention anything about the adjudicated facts. It was taken and it was mentioned only by Ms. Alaburic and not by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak. General Praljak, just a minute. General Praljak, there might have been a translation mistake, and then of course you lost your cool immediately. It probably comes from a translation mistake. It's not the first time. I note that every time we have incidents in the courtroom it comes from slight interpretation mistakes. Judge Prandler is mentioning the issue of the constitution and the dispatch of troops, and he's waiting for an answer from General Beneta. Then Ms. Alaburic suddenly stands up and is giving us a lecture on law. You can look at the transcript. She's talking about adjudicated facts. Judge Prandler never mentioned adjudicated facts. And in the translation you probably followed what Ms. Alaburic was saying and you gave us a statement, whereas Judge Prandler never mentioned all of this. He was first dealing with the question of Judge Trechsel who addressed -- which addressed a constitutional issue that had been raised by General Beneta about the compensation paid to killed soldiers. So General Beneta is the first person to talk about all this. Judge Trechsel tried to go into details, and Judge Prandler seconded that question. There was never any mention of adjudicated facts where the Chamber -- the Chamber would have admitted or not. Ms. Alaburic mentioned all this, and then you followed the -- you listened to her. So before getting all het up, please try and understand the situation and understand who's saying what. I told Ms. Alaburic that it would have been best if she had kept silent and she'd let the witness answer the constitutional issue raised by Judge Prandler before taking the floor. I believe that the way of the events unfolded here, you were -- were not understood correctly by you and then you got all nervous and all uptight for nothing. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The interpretation that I got was, "I am not convinced," says Judge Prandler, although this document says they went to Ploce, the Republic of Croatia, and no further. And you have seen that 500 witnesses responded when I called them. We did not send all the volunteers to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Out of the 500 I chose ten to send to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let's stick to facts. The document says up to Ploce, nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but this -- this, the Prosecution says, is wholly unacceptable. It started with this general trying to shout the Trial Chamber down, and it has continued with him now testifying from the dock, and both of those practices must stop straight away, in our submission -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: -- as indeed must his current attempt to shout me d own. It just has to stop because we are attempting to address these issues in a civilised way. What's happening here is the very opposite of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I hope to continue in a civilised way. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. Mr. Praljak, let Mr. Stewart speak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I don't want anybody to teach me civilised manners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm making no such attempt, Mr. Praljak. Your Honour, just to observe this, that so far as Your Honour sees that there was a question in what Judge Prandler said, I must confess it seems to be rather heavily disguised that it was a question, and it would be understandable that the witness did not see that there was a question there. So that if a learned Judge is posing a question, I entirely see that a question may often be implicit in something that the Judge says, it's probably helpful if it's made very clear to the witness that there is a question and what the question is because then he can answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, it was a question that Judge Prandler was putting. This was not acknowledgement of a constitutional issue. It was a question he was putting. General, since you have followed all that has been said, let's get back to the question that Judge Prandler was putting to you. How do you answer his question. That is what has led to this time-wasting operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would really appreciate it if the question could be repeated to me, because at first I did not understand it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: The question was related to your explanation when you said -- I cannot now find now the text, it is not an exact quotation, that the volunteers were allowed to go to Herzegovina. My question was in a way implied question, I admit, and I accept what actually Mr. Stewart said on that issue, but my question was in a way what kind of proofs you may give us that they were only allowed to go when we have seen a number of orders that they were sent to that place, I mean to Herzegovina, to the "southern front." So therefore my question is if you can cite examples and orders and all other kind of acts, official acts, which said that, "Yes, we allow those people, this or that unit, or those persons who volunteered to go." It is my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm giving evidence here from my own personal experience. If you or the Defence or anyone had thought that I should bring documents with me, I should have been told so. If you want me to bring documents, I just need some time. Right now I only have a pencil with me, and I have the experience that I carry from that war, and I have answers to questions as to how I dealt with problems, in which frameworks I had to act, and I am being asked here to interpreter documents, and I am stating my opinion about them. In all of them I see volunteers. I see orders related to the issue. I see references to cases where the state had to deal with issues related to the death of soldiers only 500 metres into Herzegovinian territory, and I had to deal with all these things. And the logic underlying this is more justified than the logic of sending troops to Afghanistan or Iraq or wherever. But with a view to our international obligations, we had to find a modality for sending their people who volunteered, who wanted to go there. Because of the workload I had in Croatia, I had to limit the number of those people, and I can only assume that Mr. Kapular, and I'm coming back to his documents because your question sublimates everything that has been said so far, all my prior experience and career, the experience on which I based my command and the experience of Mr. Kapular, are two parallel lines that never meet. Mr. Kapular, I think, came from Canada. I'm pretty sure about that. After the defence of Vukovar where he served honourably, he was given command of a brigade. I believe that for him, it was quite normal to act in a soldierly fashion and say to the men, "People, the situation there is very hard. Anyone who wants to go will have my assistance." Back in Canada his neighbour fought in Iraq or in Kuwait or in Afghanistan together with US troops. For him it must have been normal. That's why I am saying what I said about the reasons for punishing those people where he said that it was a question of professional conduct. I don't know what other things he enumerated, but the US president's speech yesterday sounded very similar to me. He brought his own life experience to that war. I believe our opinions differed even on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Beneta, I shall follow up on the two questions put by my colleagues. There was no reason for an incident to occur. When a Judge from the Bench has a question, it's important. Judge Mindua might have also put the question to you. What we would like to know is this: Whether the constitution of the Republic of Croatia enabled troops to be sent outside the Croatian state. The answer is a yes or no answer. And whether -- or in the case the constitution did not allow for that, did the constitution allow for Croatian soldiers to volunteer outside the Croatian state, which seems to be your case. This is what you told us. These are very simple questions which should not lead to a revolution. Could you answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot tell you now exactly whether the constitution made it possible or not, and if it did, which article especially, because some articles were amended, but I know that there was no grounds in the constitution for paying out benefits to a family who's father was killed outside the territory of the state, and I know I had very difficult problems at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for your answer. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. We've nearly finished this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Before we look at the next document, General, can I just take you back to the time when you were deployed in 1993 on Operation Jug. You've told us that you were there for about a week prior to the operation and for some little while after it. Before the operation, did you meet Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're going to come back to that. Would you look, please, just finishing this topic, at 4D00701, which is the last document in the binder. Very last one. This is a document dated July the 24th, and it bears the signature of Mr. Petkovic, and it's addressed to General Briquemont of UNPROFOR, and we're not going to have time to look at the whole document, but it's really on one topic. It's denying that there are HV troops in Bosnia, but saying that some had volunteered and had joined the HVO. All right? And it's going to complete this topic of volunteers on the southern front. July 24th is nine days after Operation South; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Remind us which units of the Croatian Army had been deployed in Operation South.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour, to the use of the word "remind," because the witness has never said that the operation involved units of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I think he has.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did Operation South involve units of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just tell my learned friend Mr. Laws the witness did not understand that the question is addressed to him. We, coming from our parts, are quite used to people looking us in the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, you may put your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did Operation South involve units of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation South involved the 1st Brigade of the HVO, the 3rd Brigade of the HVO, independent detachment Ludvig Pavlovic, and a group of the 5th Guards Brigade, a group of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It was a very simple question. You've listed the HVO people and finally said that there were some from the 5th Guards Brigade. They were troops of the Republic of Croatia, weren't they? We're going to look at the south in more detail later on, but just for the moment do you not agree with me that the -- even if you were to call them a group of volunteers, they were, as you were, troops from the Republic of Croatia. It's a simple yes to that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Nine days later Mr. Petkovic is writing a letter to General Briquemont in which he is denying in strong terms that troops from the Republic of Croatia have been deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina and saying that some have returned to the -- to the native homes and joined HVO units. That's halfway down page 2. Finishing this topic of Croatian involvement in Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but I did not say anything. I need time to read that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: By all means. It's quite a long letter. It's responding to something that's been said by UNPROFOR, saying that there are Croatian troops in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and General Petkovic is saying that that's not right. You take your time to look at it. He's saying that there aren't HV troops there, but there are some who have joined the HVO -- joined HVO units, I should say.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, everything that is written in this passage on page 2 is described accurately, and I have no objection to that. I think it actually corroborates all the evidence I've given here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, except for the evidence that you gave a moment ago that the 5th Guards Brigade was deployed in Operation South and that you, yourself, were on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an HV soldier. That --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. Objection to this question. The question misrepresents the fact. The witness never said that the 5th Guards Brigade was involved in the operation. The witness said that volunteers from that brigade were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, you remained a member of the Croatian Army, didn't you? You told us that yesterday. It was one of the very first questions I asked you. You remained, throughout, a member of the Croatian Army, did you not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And the members of the 5th Brigade, I don't accept for a moment that they were volunteers, but the members of the 5th Brigade remained members of the Croatian Army throughout, did they not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that operation a part of that group remained and another part returned to the Croatian Army. I also returned to the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: When they were sent to fight in Operation South, they were Croatian soldiers. That is simply the position, isn't it? Employed by -- well, look. We're going to need to get to the bottom of this. Ms. Alaburic can have the floor in just a moment, but really it's taking a great deal of time. It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I don't understand what you're doing. You intervene when the probative value of your witness will be assessed by the Judges in line with the question, the answers, and everyone's understanding of it. So wait for the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I have an objection to this question. Mr. Laws is systematically asking questions that contain inaccurate facts. You will assess whether my objection is valid or not. In line 9 of this page, the current page, Mr. Laws says that members of the 5th Guards Brigade were sent to fight in Operation South. The witness did not say that. He said that these persons were volunteers, not people who were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The people who were in Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether they got there as volunteers or whether they got there because they were sent, the members of the 5th Guards Brigade, during Operation Jug remained employees of the Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence, and HV soldiers, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that status of theirs was frozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: They were -- we are going to look at Jug in more detail later on today, but you agree with me, don't you, that they were -- the only way you can describe them is as soldiers from the HV?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and during their service there they had some aspects of that status, which was frozen at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Beneta, could you explain what you mean by "frozen"? Does it mean, for instance, that the time served in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not count as time served in the Croatian Army, for instance, for purposes of promotion or similar matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not enjoy some of the elements of their salary. We had several elements in the salary. One of them was field mission allowance payable for service in the field. If it was a short service, it did not affect the whole status. If it was a longer service, then we had cases where the man remained in the rank, the Croatian Army rank, of major, whereas he had served for a long time in Bosnia-Herzegovina and there was given the rank of brigadier. I think we have some people who are generals in Bosnia and Herzegovina, whereas in the Croatian Army they have the rank of major still, or lieutenant. So we have cases where people served for a longer spell in Bosnia and Herzegovina without being promoted in the Croatian Army. I think I can name one such person, Mr. Obradovic, and another person who remain in the area after the Operation South. He was serving in the logistics. He served there for a longer time. He received the rank of general there, but this rank is not recognised to him in the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, we're going to finish this topic now, and I'm going to suggest to you that this letter from Mr. Petkovic is doing no more than toeing the party line, putting forward the explanation that's going to be put forward for years to come and which you're still putting forward now, volunteers, not Croatian deployment, and it's not the truth, is it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are saying in my view does not reflect the situation on the ground. It's nothing that I can confirm. On the contrary, I reject that assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's turn to consider, briefly if we may, Stolac in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be better to address this after the break since it is nearly 10.30. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We're going to look briefly at the situation in Stolac in 1992 and then into 1993. When the Serbs first occupied Stolac in 1992, do you know if it is right or wrong that most of the Croat population had left Stolac shortly before the Serb arrival?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That was -- that was your understanding.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And that the majority of the Muslim population had been left behind in the town.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us a little bit about the liberation of the town from the Serbs. Are you saying that you fought your way into Stolac town and evicted the Serbs from their positions? Is that what happened in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We evicted them from the positions that they had held around Stolac and thus enabled Croats to return to Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that may be where the difference arises. There was certainly skirmishing in positions around Stolac, were there not, on the high ground?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "skirmishing."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I mean, there was some engagement between the Serbian forces and your combined forces in the hills around Stolac. That's what I mean by it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time -- to what time is the question referring?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's referring to the time immediately before the Serbs withdrew from Stolac town. Is that right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About ten days prior to that there was intensive combat activity in the area of the Dubrava plateau, which in that action was liberated by a group of soldiers, HVO soldiers, and HV soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. Let's just deal with Stolac town itself. Is it right that the Serbs left Stolac in an orderly convoy of over 70 vehicles?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many vehicles there were. I can only state that they were able to leave Stolac because we had attacked two sides out of the three that they had been keeping. One side was protected by the Bregava canyon, and they could leave by that way relatively safely, although there was fighting only a kilometre away from that road, but they couldn't be observed from anywhere, so I don't know now who left on that road, with what kind of vehicles or how many. I can only confirm that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: They left Stolac not as a result of combat operations in the town of Stolac. On that we're agreed, are we not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a military aspect it was impossible to fight in Stolac, and there shouldn't have been fighting there because Stolac is in a depression, and whoever holds the hills around it holds Stolac. You can practically choose your target if you have a rifle, and you would be only 500 metres away from it, from the positions that they had kept around Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did they, the Serbs, withdraw to the hills around Stolac, to a new front line?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They set up a new front line near the town or village of Do. They kept their positions on Mount Hrgud which is 900 metres above Stolac, and they kept their position at Zegulja and further south.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. And without being precise to the hundred metres, but roughly the Serbs remained in those positions from that withdrawal, and they remain there to this day. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. We didn't even -- we hadn't even planned to attack any further from Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, no, that's right. There was no operation mounted to drive them further back. They were still in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were they not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: But your aim was to recover the town of Stolac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and there were good reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Strategic reasons, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Strategic reasons are at a far higher level. I'm talking about reasons at the operational and tactical levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. It was a predominantly Muslim town prior to the war in 1992, 1993, was it not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of the population in the municipality of Stolac up to the war was Croatian. In the town itself, I believe that the Muslims slightly outnumbered the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I think the evidence in this case is that the municipality as a whole had 35 per cent Croats and 48 per cent Muslims, but there we are. Stolac was also a part of the Banovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which Banovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, have a look, please, at document P05237, and we'll get the answer. This is a -- in the middle of your bundle there. This is a presidential transcript, 21st of September of 1993. We're going to look at it in a different context a little bit later on, but it's the president of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman, talking to some representatives from Herceg-Bosna. And if you'd look at page 7, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's 7 in both the Croatian and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You can see a paragraph eight lines down that begins with the word "Stolac," "Stolac," full stop. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: As we can see from the text, President Tudjman speaking of Stolac: "I know the strategic importance of Stolac, both as the president of Croatia and, if you will, as a soldier. I know that Stolac and the entire former Jablanicki Kotor and Konjic were included in the Croatian Banovina in 1939. These are arguments I have upheld since the first day." And then he goes on to talk about ethnic cleansing because it's much later in time when he's speaking about this. You, as you have said, never pushed on further from Stolac.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I never tried to go further from Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The Serbs remained on their line and didn't launch an offensive to recapture the town.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. After I had given these positions to the HVO and gone south, the Serbs launched a strong counter-attack but it was unsuccessful. However, there were many casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Is it right that when you had taken control of the town from the Serbs in 1992, one of the first thing that happened was Croatian symbols and flags were put all over the town. Do you remember that happening in the time immediately after the Croatian entry into Stolac -- I'm so sorry, I should have said your entry, not the Croatian entry. You were a combined force. Immediately after the liberation of Stolac, do you recall Croatian symbols and flags being put up all over the town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot confirm that. I cannot confirm that anything dramatic of that kind was done or that it was ordered. I don't remember any such display.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: There's no suggestion that it was ordered. It's Witness DT, a 92 bis witness, who says that the first morning of your arrival in Stolac Croat flags and symbols were put all over the town. You don't recall that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look together then, please, at a document that you were shown, I think on Monday, possibly yesterday in the morning. It's P00279. It's the third document in -- in my binder as well. Stay in my binder. Third document from the front. Now, this is a document which is dated the 26th of June of 1992, and that is after the liberation of Stolac from the Serbs of which we have just been speaking, is it not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And we can see in the third paragraph that Stolac is one of the areas which is listed as being under almost the entire territory of the Croatian municipalities being under the control of the Croats. "Today we have under control almost all the entire territory of the Croatian municipalities of Neum, Ravno, Stolac, Capljina, Ljubuski, Citluk, Siroki Brijeg, and Mostar." You told us that you attended an occasion when General Petkovic made a speech, a rousing speech about problems and about their solutions. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Are you saying that this is the same text as the speech that you heard or a different text?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give a precise answer to that question. I know that General Petkovic gave a speech and that he spoke about the problems with the organisation of civilian life and the establishing of civilian life in the liberated territories and that those were the same problems that I had in the area of Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we looked at one or two of the examples of the use of the term "Croatian" in this document, but I want to look at four in all. The first we've already seen in the third paragraph down. "Today we have under control almost the entire territory of the Croatian municipalities," and then listing them in the way that we have looked at. Five lines down: "The four main tasks in front us are: "1. To put under control the remaining area of Croatian municipalities." And then 4: "To establish Croatian rule over all municipalities." I'll come back to that one in just a moment. Five paragraphs down: "Our intentions are," and then at the second bullet point: "To prepare ourselves and through offensive activities liberate the remaining Croatian territory." You said in answer to a question from one of the Judges that you didn't think that when Mr. Petkovic used the term "Croatian" he meant Croatian as opposed to Croatian and Muslim. Is that how you understand this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: How do you know what he meant, General? How do you know what he meant when he wrote those words?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from practice, because after that, on the ground -- or, rather, in the areas which Mr. Petkovic also mentions in this document, in other words, after what is said here, I established authorities in the town of Stolac on a parity level. If the Serbs had stayed, then their representatives would also have been -- would also have been included in a certain percentage, but they weren't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You're absolutely right to say that you established a joint structure in Stolac after its liberation in June of 1992. We're going to deal with that separately, just taking it very, very briefly. Sadly, you'd agree with me that didn't last more than a matter of some weeks, did it? After you left, that fell apart very quickly, didn't it? We'll look at that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot testify to the reasons of this dissolution, because after my departure I went elsewhere to deal with other problems. But what I can say here is that I did everything I did with the approval of everybody involved in that process and that nobody has ever said anything bad to me because of that, and neither was I ever condemned because of that. On the contrary, I spoke about that briefly with Mr. Petkovic. I asked him what I should do, and he gave me such suggestions, suggestions as to what I should do, because he knew the situation in that area better than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Now, I didn't ask you about the reasons why it fell apart. The fact of the matter is that it did, and we'll look at that in just a moment, I promise you, but the fact of the matter is that what you had done by way of setting up joint institutions simply didn't survive, did it? You know that as a simple fact, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that they didn't survive, but I don't know the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at that, as I say. But that doesn't help us, does it, with this document? This is addressed to a general, gentleman of the municipal leadership, and the commanders of the Croatian Defence Council units. All right? And it goes on to talk about Croatian municipalities, and under 4 it specifically says that one of the aims is -- one of the tasks is to establish Croatian rule over all municipalities. The municipalities that are being discussed here are territories within Bosnia-Herzegovina, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But territories over which the authorities of Alija Izetbegovic couldn't exert any real influence physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Territories which were claimed as part of Herceg-Bosna. That's what it comes down to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me that was a territory from which the area of the Croatian state was being attacked, and I was tasked with eliminating that threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, that's not the topic that we're dealing with here with respect to you, General. We're dealing with establishing Croatian rule over all municipalities, and you gave evidence that in your view that meant something different. We're looking at that. These are territories claimed as Herceg-Bosna, and it's only in that sense that they are Croatian territories at all, isn't it? The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can testify here about requests for me as a commander to be relieved from what today is called Simik [phoen], that is civilian military co-operation, in that area. But these tasks could have been executed only by, I believe, what was called then the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Going back to your --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could delete the Kosovo Albanians from line 18. The witness said that he supposed that the name was the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Kosovo Albanians were never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Let's go back to Stolac and your attempts to establish joint institutions between the Croats and the Muslims. You told the Chamber that there was a range of reactions from local Croats in respect of the Muslims being allowed to join in the Crisis Staff. Most were in favour and some were less favourable and some were strongly opposed to that. Does that summarise your experience in Stolac post-June 1992 accurately?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could my learned friend oblige me by referring to the exact page of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm sure I can do that in the break and I should have it with me, but the witness will remember very well what he said about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You remember, General, don't you, telling us that some -- most were in favour of joint institutions, but some were strongly opposed to Muslims being in the Crisis Staff? And you told us, do you remember, that you sent two of them away because you weren't happy with their attitude?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I really have an objection, because the witness didn't say that. The witness didn't speak about that. I object to this, and I insist that a page reference be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, the witness knows exactly what he said. General Beneta can tell the Prosecutor, "You are wrong. I never said this." It's more important to have General Beneta say this than you. Unless we think that General Beneta is totally unable to understand the questions put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, let's let him, with respect to Ms. Alaburic, let's let the General answer for himself. It's a really small detail of the evidence which he'll remember well, I suggest, and we don't need to take up more time with it. I would be very grateful if I could just continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no problem with that, and I don't doubt that General Beneta would be able to reproduce accurately what he said, but since I in my redirect have to give a page reference to the cross-examination, I think it would be fair for my learned friend to give -- state page references in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, I can do, but you know, we all have the same tools, and if it's really re-examination that's the issue here, it's 46603, line 25, and that I hope assists my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would appreciate for the gentleman to stop playing games. He knows the technique. This is what he has to do. It's not a matter of us searching for it. He has to do it. He knows it. He's been trained to do it, and we should just move on. And I think that the bench should instruct him to do that in the future as we have been instructed in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you are again insinuating improper intentions like playing games. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I'm not insinuating anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please refrain from that kind of personal attacks. It's not a matter of playing games. I don't think anyone here is playing games. It's a serious matter. Thank you for taking note.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me finish. Let me respond to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry I thought you had --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can't get a mike. If I can get a mike --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not sitting down until -- okay. Here it is. Well, first of all it is common courtesy. Second of all we need to make the record. Third, it is a game when counsel knows that he has to do it, he as at it his fingertips, and then after there's an objection and we waste five minutes, then he cavalierly says, "Well, if we must here it is." He could have done that in the first instance, and I can assure you, Judge Trechsel, being in the courtroom as a trial lawyer this is what normally has to be done by trial lawyers. They just can't say some way in the record some place and then go look for it. That must be done. This is the training that we all get in the adversarial system, and we are in an adversarial system, and I will continue to insist that on these occasions it's a mere of common courtesy so that we can all look it up because sometimes mistakes are made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, excuse me, Your Honour. I was only going to ask - I wonder if Mr. Laws would help - I don't have and others may not have the version with the full numbering. If I could either have the -- the smaller page number or some sort of fairly uniquely phrase will enable me to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. May I just say this: It's not playing games in the slightest, and I didn't have the reference to hand, and I've already apologised for that once. But this is with respect to those who are raising the objections, really a highly technical matter. The general is not misled. He knows the evidence I'm referring to. Let's proceed. If I can ask him whether he can remember it, I'll find the -- Ms. Winner sitting to my right will find the reference, I have no doubt, within the next minute or two, long before redirect takes place, and I hope that we can proceed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to say that the page and line reference given by my learned friend 46603, line 25, are about the return of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. There's been a mistake there and we'll get it in the next few minutes, I have no doubt at all we'll be able to help with the redirect which must be possibly some hours away now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: General, Beneta, is it right or is it wrong that when you formed joint institutions some people locally were opposed to the inclusion of Muslims? Is that right or wrong? Don't worry about what you said yesterday or the day before. Is that fact right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I hope that that's a sufficient basis for me to proceed now. What I'm going to suggest to you is this: Those who were opposed to it were the people who very soon after you left took control. They were the ones who didn't want to share authority with the Muslims. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood me. I said that I had spoken to the soldiers who entered Stolac or taken it militarily, if that is more acceptable to you. In that process that conversation was overheard by 400 mostly young people of Muslim ethnicity who felt attracted to the idea of establishing two battalions instead of one to defend Stolac jointly. Why did I speak to the people? Because I thought that the moment was very sensitive. One group was attacking and had jeopardised their lives to reclaim the town or the area where they were living, and others were in places held by these forces of Republika Srpska. There were indications that there might be some kind of vengeance under the assumption that the Muslims had co-operated with the Serbs. That is why devoted -- I devoted special attention to that. Those who opposed that were two soldiers. I don't think that they were significant personalities either by their education or otherwise. They didn't enjoy any special authority. They were mere soldiers, privates who didn't understand the situation well. They had some personal reasons to be opposed. And even though I tried to persuade them, they stuck to their positions. Others accepted my arguments. Most of them, if they had been asked, without my having given my introductory speech and presented my arguments, would probably have been opposed, because that was the atmosphere at the time. But they accepted what I had told them, and they understood that most probably a counter-attack would be launched. They accepted that help, and then we started organising them militarily, and I also took up measures to organise civilian administration for life to return to normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's look at life in Stolac. In October of 1992 Andjelko Markovic became the president of the HVO, and if you look at P01234, we'll see him issuing a decision in January. P01234. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I need a bit of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
