utterances.text: It's the -- possibly the fourth document in. One, two, three, four. It's with a yellow sticker, I'm told. Just probably back from where you are now. That looks like it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: 20th of January. It's the Croatian Defence Council who are, in the person of Andjelko Markovic, President of the Croatian Defence Council, issuing a decision on a curfew. All right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So it would seem the HVO exercising authority in the municipality. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I -- I really have no knowledge about this document. I cannot testify to this period to which I'm directed. I would really appreciate it if I could not be asked about documents I know nothing about and events I did not participate in, and I have nothing to say about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I just want to follow through with Mr. Markovic, if I may. Would you turn, please, in the binder to P05237. We looked at it a little while ago in the context of Stolac being in the Banovina. This is Mr. Markovic attending that very same meeting. And if you look with me, please, at page 4. We can see a paragraph in which he is speaking and he says: "Second, Stolac was twice defended as you once said, once from the Muslims and from the Chetniks." And then this: "Today there is not a single Muslim in Stolac." That's as of the 21st of September of 1993. "We have populated Stolac with our refugees from Bosnia." Can you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really beg you not to place me in a situation where I would have to confirm something I know absolutely nothing about. I was not in the area at the time. I cannot testify about anything. I don't see any reason to ask me about things I have no clue about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, if I could help you to this extent: One of the reasons you've been asked to give evidence on behalf of the Defence is to talk about attempts to set up joint institutions, and I'm exploring with you - and that's the end of, I think, the exercise - what happened, because otherwise we have the story just hanging in the air. "I did my best to set up joint institutions." They fell apart and the hardliners took control. That's the truth of it, isn't it? You must have heard about that. You were back in Bosnia the following year in 1993, weren't you? You must have known what was going on.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am really testifying to events that I was present to, events that I initiated, I have already said all I have to say about them and I'm prepared to continue to testify. Now, concerning events I was not involved in, that I knew nothing about then and still know nothing, I think I'm the wrong person to state any opinion whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, we're going to leave Stolac. Before we do so may I give everybody in the courtroom the reference that was requested, that -- the passage starts at page 466 -- sorry, 46599 at line 19, and it continues through 46600 to line 7. And in the draft I'm told it's page 66. Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I said we've finished it. We very nearly have. I want to look with you, please, at what was happening in the following April after you left Stolac. P01913. And it's a gentleman who you, I think, know, Nedeljko Obradovic. 01913. Was this the Mr. Obradovic that you were referring to earlier, Colonel Obradovic of the Knez Domagoj?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is again a document about which I can state nothing. I was not in that area of responsibility at the time, and I was in no way involved in the developments in that area. I even knew nothing about the developments in that area. I had too much to do in my area, which was the hinterland of Slano.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Could you just answer my question just -- just briefly. Was the Obradovic that we see there the one that you knew? There are several. Was this the one that you knew, the commander of the 1st Knez Domagoj?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a few men with the same name and surname, and that's why I have to ask you to relieve me from answering this question about events in which I was not involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: My question conceded that there are several people called Obradovic. I'm asking you whether you knew this one who was the commander of the 1st HVO Knez Domagoj Brigade, and being fair about it, General, you can answer that question yes or no, can't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that Nedeljko Obradovic was the commander of the 1st Brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Did you know him? Did you know this man who has put his name to this document? Was he a man that you knew? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recognise the signature, and I don't know the man well enough to identify his signature. I have to repeat, I know a man called Nedeljko Obradovic who was commander of the 1st HVO Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: General, please. You're saying you know a man called Nedeljko Obradovic who was the commander of the 1st HVO Knez Domagoj Brigade, but you're not prepared to say it's the same person. I've asked you a number of times. You know this man, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the commander of the 1st HVO Brigade who was -- who was the commander of the command of the 1st HVO Brigade and his name was Nedeljko Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. And by April 1993, according to this order, the time of joint institutions has long passed, has it not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either. At that time I was somewhere else. And please don't involve me into something that I cannot testify to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. Well, we can see that it restricts the entry of BH -- BiH Army members into the area of responsibility unless there's written clearance from the commander. Those who do are to be arrested and held for 15 days and to be disarmed. When you came back to Bosnia in 1993, was the Knez Domagoj Brigade a unit with which you had any contact?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a brigade commanded by Nedeljko Obradovic at the time that was to be involved in, in fact, one of the two main vehicles of the operation. However, that commander sent a written report that he did not have the required forces for the mission. Did he not come to the command, and I suppose it was also a matter of personal differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Well, let's move on to 1993, the time when you came to Bosnia, and you said yesterday you thought you were coming to fight the Serbs and only found out later that you were coming to engage Muslim forces. Yes?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Would you look with me, please, at Exhibit P03112. This is a document dated the 2nd of July of 1993. It's another presidential transcript. We can see that those present include Mr. Susak and General Bobetko. And we're going to pick it up at page 54. There's a discussion at the top of that page about sanctions, and then five lines down the conclusion that Tudjman has reached that "I think this threat is even smaller today but we must be careful not to give them any direct cause to serve as an excuse for their policy." And then this: "Clearly we must not do this. But at the same time we must take steps to protect Croatian interests in the territorial sense too. And, you two please, Minister Susak, General Bobetko, see about this and meet with Herceg-Bosna leaders there, with General Praljak, Petkovic and Ambassador Sancevic and their leaders there, with Boban and Prlic to discuss exactly what should be done. But it goes without saying, do not lead the operation in such a way as to make it a direct involvement. And what I said earlier is very important in terms of, I don't know, of trade, of payments, I don't know what, do not let the people there feel left on their own but let's take care in this respect." If you turn on two pages, please, you'll see that later on in the conversation that day, it's our page 67, President Tudjman has something to say about the southern Neretva front. "Still on the southern Neretva front, it's important for us to push back Muslim units, and if we do this, it will be a sign for the Serbs not to move." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: This is the 2nd of July, which is just short of two weeks away from Operation South in which you were involved, is it not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a -- this is 13 days before the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I wasn't there. I wasn't there at that meeting, but I wasn't even in the area of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, you were involved in the operation that took place two weeks later, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two weeks later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you understand that General Bobetko was the person in overall control of that operation, Operation Jug or South?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing during the time I was there that gave me basis to conclude something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. But we'll look at a document in just a moment in respect of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, very briefly. On page 67, I read what President Tudjman said. He mentions the southern front, but I have the feeling that he is breaking down this operation in two parts, A, the Muslim parts, and then he adds that this could be a sign for the Serbs not to move, or a signal for the Serbs not to move. In military terms, the operation against the Muslims, well, does it have an impact on the Serbs as well by demonstrating their strengths against the Muslims this would prevent the Serbs from moving. What do you think about this? I'm just talking in military terms, of course.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the fear from the south part of Croatia being cut off was extremely strong among the Croatian leadership at the time. The easiest way -- because the greatest majority of roads and in the Neretva River valley. In addition to that, the Ploce port was the only one with sufficient capacity to support the entire hinterland. For that reason, but also based on intelligence reports and because of that previously mentioned S-2 plan, this thinking was justified for the State of Croatia, in my only personal estimate, the enemy were the Serbs associated with the Yugoslav People's Army, both from Serbia and Republika Srpska, because it was they who, from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were threatening the Croatian territory, which is militarily practically undefendable south of the Neretva River, especially if you don't go across the border at least up to Popovo Polje. That's why there was a little -- a lot of military concern about this invasion. As the Muslim forces grew in strength, they also obviously wanted to reach lines in the Neretva River valley, and some intelligence reports that I heard when I was in command reconnaissance indicated that. It was a surprise to me. I also heard of events north of Mostar that caused me a lot of concern. I believe that the name is Bijelo Polje. And they pointed out that the situation was very grave indeed. Croatian forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I believe, according to a uniform, widely shared judgement and estimate based on the same premises concluded that this was a possibility. And I participated in that operation defending approaches to the Neretva River valley, because I had already liberated that area once. And believe me when I say that I was not at all looking forward to doing it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We saw that it was General Bobetko who was present at that meeting with President Tudjman when there was discussion about doing something to protect Croatian interests, and I'm going to take you now to an interview which was held between the Office of the Prosecutor and Brigadier Dzanko in July of 2003. Now, Luka Dzanko was the gentleman to whom you reported. He's the man who asked you whether you wanted to come to Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Will you turn, please, in the binder to the last-but-one document, P11070. Right at the back, two documents in.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend. I just want my objection on the record. This is a new document not on the 65 ter list, and I would appreciate it if my learned friend Mr. Laws, in keeping with the decision of the Trial Chamber from last year, would explain the reason for introducing this document, and also I hope the Trial Chamber will rule on admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, may I say that's a matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Let me recall that the Trial Chamber has handed down guidelines and stated clearly that when a document is not on the 65 ter list, the party using this document uses it only to test the credibility of the witness. This has been stated many a time. Every time this document comes up we are told the same thing. What's the point ever issuing guidelines in that case? Please proceed, Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: May I say that that's an issue which is currently being litigated by way of IC lists which the Prosecution hope will bring some clarity to that issue, but for the moment if I can continue with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The meeting in the presidential palace was the 2nd or 3rd of July, and I want to pick the story up now with General Bobetko calling Brigadier Dzanko on the 5th of July. We're dealing with Operation Jug and with its origins, and then we're going to look at happened in it, all right? P11070. If you look with me --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. When Mr. Laws says it's a matter of currently being litigated, what is he saying? Is he saying he's not going to comply with the guidelines or that he is complying with the guidelines and then he's going to say how he's complying with the guidelines? I'm just not clear. He brushed it aside very deftly, but it was a bit of a brushing aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I didn't brush anything aside. I was invited to take the floor and continue with this by the President who said that every time this issue arises time is taken up with this, and I was invited to continue and that's what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I -- nevertheless, the "Please proceed Mr. Laws" from Your Honour preceded Mr. Laws giving any answer at all in relation to the objection, and Your Honour specifically referred to the Trial Chamber's own guidelines without any answer having been given as to how those guidelines are actually being complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The answer, Mr. President, is the one you gave: That I'm using this document in one way at the moment, and if I seek its submission by way of an IC list in due course, that's a matter the Chamber will rule. But nothing prevents me from using this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, it's -- Mr. Laws could -- one assumes he could easily simply say "I'm using it for this purpose or that purpose in compliance with the guidelines." It's a single sentence. He must know presumably. I'm sure he knows. Mr. Laws knows what he's doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, Mr. Stewart always intervenes to say something useful. He is asking you to tell him in line with the guidelines that you are using this document to test the credibility of the witness. That is all Mr. Stewart is asking you to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, without getting too deeply into the guidelines and precisely what their application involves, the Prosecution's submission is that they do not require us at this stage to make statements about the purpose with which the document is being used. I can say straight away that this witness gives an account of this event which differs from the account that this record of interview discloses. So to that extent at this stage, I am addressing the credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, I don't agree with you. We have a document that is not on the 65 ter list, that the Defence quite rightly raises the issue. The Defence teams are right. Second point. The guidelines of the Chamber clearly indicate that in such a case the party using such a document uses it solely for the purpose of testing the credibility of the witness. That's it. So in line with the guidelines, you should say, "I wish to use this document to check a number of points the witness has indicated which relate to his own credibility." Maybe this document contradicts what he said a while ago, what he stated yesterday. This is what Mr. Stewart would like to know, and he's right. And you are trying to bypass the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: With the greatest of respect I'm not trying to bypass anything at all, and the guidance of the Appeals Chamber on this topic is the subject of current litigation before the Chamber. The Appeals Chamber have made it clear that the use of a document of this kind is not limited to testing the credibility. Can I leave it in this way: At the moment I'm going to explore with this witness the issue of his credibility so far as the preparations of Operation Jug goes. I reserve my right as to any other use that the Prosecution may wish to make of it in due course, but I hope that assists Mr. Stewart at the moment. May I now proceed to use the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being you are testing the credibility of the witness, and I would like the legal officer to pull out the decision handed down by the Appeals Chamber, who seems to be stating -- which seems to be stating the contrary. So please proceed on the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Do you have the paragraph beginning -- 667, number 667: "On the 5th of July, 1993, I was called by General Janko Bobetko." Do you have that line?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: "On the 5th of July knee I was called by General Janko Bobetko who then was the head of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army. He told me to come to the command post in Zadar and he gave me the oral order to go to Neum in BiH. To be in Neum on the 7th of July, 1993, in the morning, in the municipal building, and to wait for him on the same location on the 8th of July. He said to me that I was entitled to take two officers with me, based on my personal choice, to be my assistants in operational duties. I chose Colonel Ivan Beneta and Colonel Davorin Radic." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Do you agree with your brigadier so far that that's what he did in choosing you and the captain who he names there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the only thing that I can confirm of all this, that I was asked by Mr. Dzanko to take part in this operation, and it's true that this other colleague was there, Davorin Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And you have testified that Milivoj Petkovic was not someone you had met prior to Operation Jug; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. I hadn't seen Mr. Petkovic before the operation, nor did I see him during or after it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what Brigadier Dzanko says starting at line 683 about the meeting on the 8th of July in Neum. "General Bobetko came. He held the meeting on which there were present Milivoj Petkovic, HVO head of staff, General Martic, his deputy, Stanko Martic from the HVO; and a Colonel called Pranjo [phoen] Pavicic. General Bobetko's brought Pavicic from the Croatian Army school as the expert for artillery. I was present, Beneta was, as well as Radic from the Croatian Army. And the topic of that meeting was Operation Jug, which I will give more details about later as a special issue." Do you agree with me that the brigadier appears to be saying there something very different to you; namely, that Mr. Petkovic was present at a meeting in Neum to discuss Operation Jug?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm or provide an explanation because in spite of what is stated here, I was not at that meeting. At the time, I probably hadn't even left Zadar. I arrived on the 8th very late in the evening. I only slept at Neum and on the next morning I continued to the command post. Your Honours, I was familiarised with this document during the proofing by counsel Ms. Alaburic. I found not only this inaccuracy but more of them in the memory of Mr. Dzanko about the establishing of the battalion at Stolac and some other situations that he sees very differently from the way I see them and the way I remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Because it's your assertion that Petkovic is not involved in Operation Jug, and you're not going to agree with the brigadier's recollection as expressed in this document that you had a chance to see the other day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you misinterpreted my words. I have said several times, and I'm going to repeat it again, I did not meet Mr. Petkovic or Mr. Bobetko either before, during, or after Operation South. I don't believe that I ever met Mr. Bobetko either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The taking of Blagaj was one of the key objectives of Operation South, was it not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key objective of the reduced operation was to cut through the area between Heliodrom and Gnojnice, the consequence of which would have been that the forces to the south would be cut off and their status would have been resolved in negotiations. We were -- we did not favour the taking of such a wide area or an operation that would involve the taking of Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You say that you didn't favour it. At what stage do you say you learnt about the fact that South was an attack on Muslim forces, before coming to Neum or after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that was something I learned at the command reconnaissance mission which took place at the hill next to Krivodol, and from there we had a good overview of the situation in the Mostar valley from the winery or the Heliodrom if a -- that's -- if that's your favourite, all the way to Buna or the airstrip.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes. The question I asked you is did you learn about the fact that South was an attack on Muslim forces before coming to Neum or after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I learned that not at Neum but only after I had left and gone to the field in the area of Krivodol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you that question again, and it may be there's a problem with the translation. Did you learn that Operation South was an attack on Muslim forces before arriving at Neum or after you had arrived?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about it after I had left Neum. In other words, not at Neum but after spending the night there and leaving Neum. So I learned these things not at Neum but at Krivodol. The objective of the operation was something about which I heard in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So having chosen you as one of his two assistants, Dzanko held a meeting in Neum which you didn't attend, and by that stage, with a week to go before the operation, hadn't told you, his assistant, that it was the Muslims, not the Serbs, who were the target. Is that really what you are saying to us, General?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before replying, I must correct you. I was not his deputy. I was the third man down. That is, Chief of Staff. You said deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. I didn't call you deputy even once. I said you were one of his assistants. It doesn't matter. The question still stands. Could you please answer it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't his assistant either. I was Chief of Staff, no more, no less. And at Neum he didn't inform me what it was about. It was only at Krivodol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to deal with the outcome of Operation South, if we may. It was an attack that took place -- it was an attack that took place on the 15th of July, which had been the subject, as you call it, of some sabotage operations which held it up for a day or two; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Beneta, just a small detail. Whilst Mr. Laws was putting questions to you, I was re-reading the decision of the Chamber, as well as my dissident opinion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: My dissenting opinion, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I was also reading the questions put by Mr. Scott to Luka Dzanko, and I note one thing: Luka Dzanko seems to be saying that at this meeting in Neum held on July 8th, 1998 -- 1993, excuse me, you were present. Were you there? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the interview held with Mr. Dzanko -- or, rather, in that interview I saw some false statements about my name and about that period, one of them being that I did not come to Neum with him. And I couldn't have attended the meeting because I arrived very late. And he sent me to the area of Krivodol in the morning to find an adequate spot and that he would follow with the task. I as Chief of Staff was tasked to establish a command post from which the operation would be led, and that's what I did. I found other inaccuracies, too, involving my name. I did not check when this statement was taken, but it is obvious that it is partly incorrect as -- as far as it involves me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wanted to check that. Mr. Laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: We were just going to deal with what you termed the sabotage operations that delayed Operation South, and I want to take you back to a document that you looked at yesterday with Ms. Alaburic in the morning. It's in the other binder, and it's P10145.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: 10145. It's in fact the last document in the binder if that helps you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You were taken to part of this statement about the attempts that it specifies to conduct or to call sabotage operations. I want to start, please, by looking at paragraph 23 where this gentleman describes special HVO units coming to arrest him and his colleagues. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Paragraph 23?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to inform my learned friend that the Croatian version doesn't have paragraph numbers. So if you could refer to the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I'm close. Just tell me the first words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It's page 4, and it's the second paragraph up on that page. "Until the 30th of June, 1993, there were 130 soldiers ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And it describes that special HVO units came to address them, and then if you skip the next paragraph, the arrest is described. It's over the page for you on page 5. "I was woken by a soldier aiming his weapon at my neck. The whole unit was disarmed. We were made to get into a truck and brought to Dretelj about 11.00 on 30th of June, 1993." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: You were asked to comment on this. Were you aware of the order that had been issued to detain Muslim members of the HVO and Muslim men of military age? Were you aware of that order?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: When you were fighting in Operation Jug, were you aware of any orders as to the detention of men who you encountered? Muslim men.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unclear about the period to which you're referring. Do you mean the events mentioned here at which I was not present, or do you mean the sabotage actions between the planned beginning of the operation and the actual beginning of the operation, because the two -- there is no connection between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: My question, I don't think, could really relate to either of those. It says when you were fighting in Operation Jug, when your men -- when the -- when the forces engaged in Operation Jug fought on the 15th of July, were you aware of any orders as to the detention of the men whom you encountered, Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you. You gave as your opinion the view that the commander faced with this sort of situation as described in the statement P10145, you gave us your opinion that it was justifiable to take the steps that he took to protect his own troops and to protect the civilian population. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that there was question from the Bench about the way a commander should act to take care of civilians in operations generally, and reducing the probability of casualties among civilians. But I understood neither that question nor my reply to refer to any concrete events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Very well. In this statement, if you turn, please, to page 8. Can you see a paragraph in the middle of the page dealing with the 15th of July, retrieving the body of this gentleman's cousin, Remza Ulakovic? Can you see that? Did I say a page number? I'm sorry, page 7, right in the middle. Page 7, right in the middle.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And if we read on, we can see the reference to at least 50 people being killed, trampled to death or dying through exhaustion. That's three paragraphs down. And then reference to this gentleman's grandmother, Fata Sabljic, who was 94 years old and who was also expelled. She could only walk very slowly. Do you agree with me that from a military point of view, civilians of that kind present absolutely no threat to soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And so to expel them from their homes can't ever be justified, can it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree. There are military situations in which collecting people, gathering them in one place, is justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: But what's being described here is a woman of 94 who is being expelled, who can only walk very slowly. She's not being collected for her own safety. This is something which a military commander has no business doing. It's no part of soldiering, is it, forcing people out of their homes at that age. Is it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must go back to my reply of yesterday. Obviously I didn't explain the situation well enough. Your Honours, most houses, especially in villages on the Dubrava plateau, and this is the area concerned here, so most of these houses are one-storey houses. They only have a ground floor. They have roofs, slanting roofs of brick tiles, and there is a ceiling that is made of reed without any concrete. When we come to a village in which civilians can only have such kind of shelter, generally speaking it is easier to collect these people, take them to a safe place, because you never know where a shell from a mortar or a cannon can land. And the other supply routes are cut. The people can't go even out to their yards to fetch water from their wells. So it is more logical, and it's justified to take all these people to one place and take care of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, could you explain the logic behind taking away the Muslim but not Croat people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see no mention of the taking care of Croats in this statement. This is a statement given by a Muslim witness which gives information about himself and other Muslims. I do not read this to mean that nobody took care of the Croats. On the contrary. I strongly doubt that the Croats remained in such houses whereas the Muslims were forced out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: But you've read this statement. It's about forcing people, not just from their homes but expelling them to Blagaj. Look at the paragraph immediately above the assessment that 50 people were killed, trampled to death. "At the beginning of the expulsions from Buna to Blagaj there were casualties every day, but later on the HVO soldiers stopped firing systematically on the exiled people." It's nothing to do with taking care of people, collecting them, looking after them. It's expelling them and shooting them, shooting at them systematically. That's what this witness statement describes. Can you confirm for us that a commander has no, no justification for behaving in that way at any time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I would qualify that with assuming the facts that are being described in this document are correct, because that's what the witness is being asked to assume. When it comes from the Prosecutor's mouth it's as if these are the facts, so assuming the facts are correct, with that proviso I would say that the question then is proper; otherwise, it assumes facts not in evidence and the question is improper, and I would object to that question being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I -- I don't mind the intervention at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Assume the facts are true, that these HVO soldiers are expelling civilians, including women of 94 and forcing them to walk to Blagaj and then shooting at them. Assume that's true. No commander has any business doing anything of that kind ever, do they?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm told that might and appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's time for the break, but you only have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. One moment we have two IC numbers first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution has submitted their objections to documents tendered for admission by 4D and 3D through Witness Milan Gorjanc. The documents submitted shall be given Exhibit IC1102 and 1103 respectively. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Laws, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: General, we'll just finish off with the remaining time the questions that I have in respect of Operation South or Jug, please. Just to recap, we saw the presidential transcript, which is the 2nd of July, talking about what needed -- whatever needed to be done with General Bobetko. I put to you the 8th of July meeting in respect of that operation in Neum, and you've given us your evidence about that. Can we just look, please, at one document in the Prosecution binder, the smaller of the two binders, and it's P03128. And it's an order from General Petkovic in agreement, so it says, with the head of the Defence Department, Bruno Stojic, and I wonder if you'd look with me, please, at the heading "Sector South," which is the fourth heading on the document. For you it's the foot of page 2 and then going over the page to page 3. In the English it's the second page of the document. And the third sub-heading, sub-heading "Task." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: This involves General Petkovic discussing the taking of land in the same area as the later Operation South was to take place. Do you agree? You particularly mentioned the village of Gnojnice and we talked about Blagaj. It's the area south of Mostar, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I believe the witness received a wrong interpretation. What he heard was Operation Storm instead of Operation South. Just to avoid misunderstanding his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. I'm not suggesting that General Petkovic was involved in Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: The Operation South objectives were to take the area south of Mostar, as you've told us. Specifically you made reference a moment ago to the village named there of Gnojnice; is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is a technical error on behalf of the Prosecution. This is not about Operation South. It is about Sector South. I would appreciate it if the Prosecutor would read exactly what is written. There are three sectors mentioned, north, centre, and south. There is no Operation South in this document. This must be a slip of the tongue. He got carried away with Operation South and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: I've not suggested that this document has mentioned Operation South nor I hope am I carried away. I'm simply identifying the objectives as expressed in this document, and General Petkovic will have a full opportunity to testify about this in due course. But on the 2nd of July, this document appears to specify certain objectives. What I'm doing with the witness is clarifying that they overlap with and are very similar to the expressed objectives of Operation South. Not that this is South, but that this is aiming at, in particular, areas that were later to be the target of South.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: And that's right, General, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about this document, because I can't see in it anything I could testify to. I was not there at the time. I've never seen this document before. I was not aware of its existence, and I can't see anything here in my role as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Forgive me. On Monday you testified about witness statements taken under interrogation. You testified about the friendship agreement. You've testified about a range of things of which you have absolutely no presence at all. This is a question based on this document, and I'm asking you to confirm what I suggest is the plain obvious truth, that the objective set out in "Task" under 3 are the objectives, some of the objectives of Operation South. Particularly, you mentioned Gnojnice village, and we talked, you and I, about Blagaj village and clearing the area south of Mostar. That's all. And you can comfortably do that if you choose to do so, General, can you not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you can find in the documentation from that area hundreds of documents referring to these places, because every military document describing the situation in the terrain refers to key points and features on the ground. You can find reams of documents of this kind. You can't use them to prove that this is linked to an operation or anyone's intent. I'm not saying yes or no. I'm just saying I can't say anything on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Could you not worry about what I'm trying to prove or what I'm not trying to prove. I'm simply trying to establish the fact that on the 2nd of July, General Petkovic is expressing an intention in securing the objectives which later were the express intention of Operation South itself. I'm not saying it is Operation South. I'm asking you to confirm that, and if you decline to do so, then that's a matter for you. We'll move on. Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say on the basis of this document or this idea I can't confirm or deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Even though it has the place names that we've discussed, are you actually trying to help us at this stage, General, or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm really trying to be helpful about things that I was involved in, that I knew something about, but this is not the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: All right. You've been brought to court partly to say that General Petkovic was not involved in Operation South, and what I'm doing is looking with you at whether he was expressing an interest in the objectives, whether he was present at the meeting in Neum which you say you were not present at when Operation South was discussed, and now I'm going to look with you at a document that may have another connection to this operation. Would you turn, please, to look at -- at document P03466. And paragraph -- the paragraph that we need to look at, please, is in the English at the foot of page 2, the paragraph beginning "Out of 700 men," and in the B/C/S it is a paragraph just to the right of the lower hole punch, beginning "Out of 700 men from the battalion of the 5th Guards." Do you see that paragraph? Can you see that paragraph, General?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. This one begins with "The 3rd Brigade numbers 750 men."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: No. If you go down just another six lines, you'll see just the right of the lower hole punch: "Out of 700 men from the battalion of the HV 5th Guards Motorised Brigade --" got that one?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: There's a trap in this document because in English it says, "During the attack on the 10th of July," you can see in the B/C/S that it's the 15th of July, can you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Before you answer, you have no time left, Mr. Laws. The witness will answer and that's when we shall stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've just been told that I have three minutes left according to our calculation. May I just complete this document and then draw it to a close? I'll be no more than another minute or so, but I want to just get this clear. It's the end of Operation South.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: 15th of July is in the document, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall just turn to my colleagues to see whether we will grant you an extra few meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have no time left. The Trial Chamber generously grants you three extra minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I'm very grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: 15th of July. What's being described in this letter is the attack on the 15th of July in the area south of Mostar, its task being to cut off the Muslim forces and take Gnojnice, a village you and I discussed a just a moment ago. During very heavy fighting, the brigade had 12 dead and 30 wounded, of whom three soldiers were seriously injured. The infantry part was pulled out of combat and put up in a hotel in Neum, et cetera. Now, that's a report about the short-lived and unsuccessful operation that was Operation South, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: It couldn't possibly be anything else, could it? That's what it is.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read it through. I just read the passage you pointed out. If you want to ask me about the whole document I'd have to read the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: That's the only passage that we need and that, I think you agree, relates to the short-lived unsuccessful Operation South. This is a document which is being sent to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and the Main Staff of the Croatian Army by two people, Milivoj Petkovic as the Chief of the Main Staff, and Luka Dzanko the brigadier who was, as you have told us, in charge of the operation from the Croatian side. All right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, judging by the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: So just drawing the strands together, you've come here partly to say that Petkovic was not responsible or involved in Operation Jug, and here he is reporting on that day about what had happened in relation to it. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BENETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this I can also see that just as Mr. Dzanko, Mr. Petkovic was angry about certain aspects of this situation. Mr. Dzanko, after we finalised that day, I believe he went somewhere else that evening, he told me the next day, this document had been drafted, that he had invited General Petkovic to help him assess the situation, and in my recollection General Petkovic was extremely angry about the whole situation, but for more details you should ask someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAWS
utterances.text: Well, we hope to, but for what it's worth, that is the end of my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, before we give the floor to the Petkovic Defence for redirect, I'd like to remain on this document, and I ask you to look at the end of the document where General Petkovic makes proposals. When he testifies, we shall, of course review this document again, but I would like to put you this question. I see that General Petkovic analyses the situation and explains that the Chetniks, let's say the Serbs, and the Muslim forces are occupying a strategic axis which is the road from Stenovac [phoen] to Drenovic, I'm sorry we don't have a map, and the ultimate objective is the Neretva and the Ploce harbour. In this document General Petkovic puts the Serbs and the Muslims on the same side, i.e., the enemy, and he specifies, as you can see in this document, that the situation seems to call for, on the part of the Croatian Army the taking of the Bregava River and of the Popovo Polje area. And then in the second part of the document General Petkovic seems to be writing that in order to liberate the Neretva valley, let's say the Mostar-Jablanica area, that's what's written here, it would be necessary, seemingly, for the forces of the HVO to be reinforced by professional brigades of the Croatian Army. When I see this - and I listened very carefully, as you can well imagine, to all the questions put by the Prosecutor on Operation South - I have the feeling, which of course merits further investigation, that on the side of the HVO and the Croatian Army the positioning of the Serb forces was an issue, and this is actually what is written in the document. At the time you were there, during this Operation South was the Serb issue the key issue or was it the Muslim issue which was the key issue or were they both key issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, Your Honour, the level of threat was the same from the Serbian side, and a new threat seemed to be emerging, namely that Muslims, too, might be looking to get to the Neretva River valley up to Ploce. So it was both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as you're concerned, there are two threats. Ms. Alaburic, normally speaking you had nine minutes left for your redirect. Of course, if you go beyond that time, it will be taken off your overall time, so you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of General Petkovic believes that we have gotten the Trial Chamber used to using up all our time to the last minute and more, but this time we have no redirect. Thank you, Witness, for your answers. Thank you for coming to The Hague. I hope to see you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in light of the fact that your testimony has just come to an end, I would like to thank you for having come to testify at the request of the Defence counsel to help us establish the truth. I wish you a safe journey home, and I shall ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we have a few minutes left before adjourning, Ms. Alaburic, you have planned to bring a witness for next week. Everything is running smoothly, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from what I know now, the witness is coming tomorrow. He will be ready to come into the courtroom on Monday. He will be continuing with the subject of Stolac at the beginning of the Muslim-Croat conflict, and we can expect to spend four or five days in the courtroom with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have planned to hear him for three hours. Other Defence counsel have an hour and a half, and the Prosecutor will have three hours. That is what has been scheduled. This is what you have provided us with. I shall ask the registrar to move into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, do you have anything to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me. Yes. Thank you, Mr. President, and greetings to Your Honours and to all. We've got another down day tomorrow. We had two down days last week. I think we've sat for a combined total of 24 days during September and October. We're proceeding at a glacial pace, and it's become in the view of the Prosecution grossly inefficient and a waste of the Court's resources. May we invite the Petkovic team to have the following witness on standby and in The Hague next week in the event that, as we did this week, the three-hour witness for direct has actually concluded his testimony in three days so that we're able to make full use of the Court's time and resources and to proceed more expeditiously through the Petkovic case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me to say just this: If all the Defence teams had availed themselves of their right to cross-examine, we would have entered the fourth day of examination of this witness as we had planned. When scheduling our witnesses, we also reckon with the Judges' questions, and we did this on the basis of the duration of Judges' questions in the past. We think it appropriate for Judges to have enough time to examine our witnesses as well while we are all relatively relaxed, without feeling under pressure while contemplating our questions. I believe that the next witness will take a longer time. There will be many more controversial issues covered, and there will be many more Judges' questions, we expect. If you instruct me to reduce the expected time for each witness and to reckon with a reduced time for the Judges' questions and if the Court is prepared to pay for witnesses being here on standby, I will be happy to obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, let me give me -- my opinion on this also. I am very interested by all the trials that occur here, and I note that the pace of Defence witnesses is always different from the pace of Prosecution witnesses, and all trials experience this. When it comes to the Defence case, things become more complicated. Why is it? Well, because the Defence must contact the witnesses, then convince them to come and testify. These are usually witnesses that are high ranking in the administration, in the military, or in politics. So everything is complicated for the Defence. And I also note that up until now it's true that we've had some down days, but I believe that the trial is still proceeding at a very good pace. And just as Ms. Alaburic justly said, the witness could have been -- could have continued to testify tomorrow. The other Defence teams decided that they didn't want to cross-examine, but they could have done so. And even during the Prosecution case, we had some Prosecution witnesses that end up -- ended their testimony earlier than expected. So I believe that we are running at a very good pace. We're almost at three-fourths of the trial. We still have 20, 25 per cent of total time to finish in time. We're not running late. The Trial Chamber has taken into account the fact that a few -- that sometimes some accused were not present in the courtroom, but fortunately their counsel were representing them so we could continue whereas we might have decided for a stay. So I think that we are really trying to move forward. Everyone is trying to move forward. The schedule that we have been provided with is very good, and I believe that we should stick to it. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I've expressed what is the Prosecution's submission on this. We're three and a half years into this trial. I think that what has been the exception and the -- the consequence or the circumstance to be avoided, whether it was during the Prosecution case or the Prlic case or the Stojic case or the Praljak case, was to not have these gaps in the trial becoming the rule, and it appears to us that is -- that's really now what is becoming the accepted or the customary practice during, admittedly, this early phase of the Petkovic trial. Obviously, every team and everybody recognising that there are scheduling issues and time runs on. I think in terms of practice in the other trials it's the witness who waits. In this case it seems to be more so now than ever that it's the Judges and the parties, really, who wait. We're all waiting now for the next few days until the next witness is here ready to go, when, in fact, perhaps the witness should be the one has a wait a little longer for the preceding witness to conclude his or her testimony. So we obviously acknowledge the views of the President, but nonetheless, I think that I am expressing some valid concerns on the part of the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, we're today November 11th. Courtroom I, no trial. Courtroom II, Stanisic was sitting this morning and the afternoon there will be no sitting. November 11th, Courtroom number III, Prlic in the morning, nothing in the afternoon. Check with the other Trial Chambers, the ones that are also running trials. For them also it's difficult to have witnesses and so on. I believe that the Prlic trial is the one where there's the less down time, contrary to what you've just stated. Let's put an end to this. We will resume next Monday, 2.15 p.m., with the Defence witness called by the Petkovic team. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 16th day of November, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
